query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, the initially metastable solid-solution state is transformed upon thermal exposure via a kinetically controlled nucleation and growth pathway that precipitates fine, Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. When these nanoprecipitates remain finely dispersed and coherent with the matrix, they help retain corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation resistance by limiting rapid internal diffusion and preventing the formation of continuous, deleterious intermetallic networks. If the precipitation kinetics accelerate excessively (e.g., under prolonged or higher-temperature exposure), coarsening into a contiguous intermetallic network occurs and degrades the protective performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing Mg-bearing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Thermal aging treatments at controlled temperatures representing service conditions (e.g., moderate temperature aging vs. high-temperature aging) to trigger the transformation.
generation.conditions: A controlled comparison between samples maintained at a moderate service temperature (e.g., <400 °C) and those exposed to higher temperatures (e.g., >700 °C) over defined durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, size, and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates (nanoscale in one case, coarser in the other) that mediate the passivating element partitioning at the microstructural level.
generation.mechanism: The metastable solid solution gradually decomposes via nucleation and growth of intermetallic phases. When finely dispersed, these precipitates act as barriers to rapid diffusion and maintain a beneficial element partitioning (potentially promoting stable oxide or passivation layer formation). However, if growth is uncontrolled, coalescence into a continuous intermetallic network creates preferential paths for oxidation and localized corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Moderate thermal aging will yield a fine, coherent dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallic nanoprecipitates with minimal loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state, while higher-temperature or overaged conditions will produce coarser intermetallic networks leading to degraded protective properties.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, metastable solid-solution state exhibiting initial corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: Service regimes are defined by temperature: below ~400 °C where limited kinetics favor fine nanoprecipitate formation versus above ~700 °C where enhanced kinetics drive coarsening into continuous intermetallic phases.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical temperatures and aging durations to distinctly separate the regimes, as well as the quantitative relation between intermetallic size/distribution and the extent of corrosion/oxidation resistance loss, remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to moderate aging (e.g., 350–400 °C for a fixed time) and another set to high-temperature aging (e.g., >700 °C) for comparable durations. Characterize the microstructure via TEM/SEM to determine the size, coherence, and distribution of intermetallic precipitates. Perform electrochemical corrosion tests and high-temperature oxidation tests (under simulated service conditions) on both sets alongside as-cast controls.
measurements: TEM/SEM imaging to quantify intermetallic particle size and network formation
XRD for phase identification and evolution
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., polarization resistance, impedance) for corrosion
High-temperature oxidation weight gain or scale integrity tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If moderate aging does not yield a fine, coherent dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates (or if no significant difference in corrosion/oxidation performance is observed compared to the as-cast state) or if high-temperature aging does not lead to the formation of a coarser, continuous intermetallic network with degraded protective properties, then the hypothesized mechanism would be falsified.

The Effects of the Al and Zr Contents on the Microstructure Evolution of Light-Weight AlxNbTiVZry High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractTo investigate the comprehensive effects of the Al and Zr element contents on the microstructure evolution of the AlNbTiVZr series light-weight refractory high entropy alloys (HEAs), five samples were studied. Samples with different compositions were designated Al1.5NbTiVZr, Al1.5NbTiVZr0.5, AlNbTiVZr, AlNbTiVZr0.5, and Al0.5NbTiVZr0.5. The results demonstrated that the actual density of the studied HEA samples ranged from 5.291 to 5.826 g·cm−3. The microstructure of these HEAs contains a solid solution phase with a BCC structure and a Laves phase. The Laves phase was further identified as the ZrAlV intermetallic compound by TEM observations. The microstructure of the AlNbTiVZr series HEAs was affected by both the Al and Zr element contents, whereas the Zr element showed a more dominant effect due to Zr atoms occupying the core position of the ZrAlV Laves phase (C14 structure). Influence of Zirconium on the Microstructure, Selected Mechanical Properties, and Corrosion Resistance of Ti20Ta20Nb20(HfMo)20−xZrx High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractThe presented work considers the influence of the hafnium and molybdenum to zirconium ratio of Ti20Ta20Nb20(HfMo)20−xZrx (where x = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 at.%) high-entropy alloys in an as-cast state for potential biomedical applications. The current research continues with our previous results of hafnium’s and molybdenum’s influence on a similar chemical composition. In the presented study, the microstructure, selected mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance were investigated. The phase formation thermodynamical calculations were also applied to predict solid solution formation after solidification. The calculations predicted the presence of multi-phase, body-centred cubic phases, confirmed using X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy. The chemical composition analysis showed the segregation of alloying elements. Microhardness measurements revealed a decrease in microhardness with increased zirconium content in the studied alloys.
